metadata.text: Operational Requirements Safety & Security S&S/ FireSafety /OR/FSM/ Doc1.1/Nov24 1/12 Fire Safety Management Requirements Relevant Brand Safety Standards: A documented Emergency and Evacuation Plan is required. The plan must consider the requirements of people with Disabilities. [55945] • Emergency response training must be given to all staff with duties related to emergency or evacuation situations. [1131432] • Colleagues including contract and temporary, must receive training in the plan at least once every six months [1131433] • The plan must be reviewed at least annually and upon Significant Change. [1131434] • Evacuation Drills must be held at least once every six months and include those who work at night. [1131435] • Every 12 months, the Evacuation Drill must involve the use of the fire alarm and detection system. [1131436] Emergency Egress must be possible through exit doors at all times [ 56058] Storage is not permitted in Emergency Egress [56 317] • Storage rooms / closets must not open into Emergency Egress stairwells. [56318] Flammable Materials stored in the main building or any of the interior corridor guest room areas of a hotel must be kept in fire proof lockers or cabinets of a minimum of 30 minutes fire resistance. [56720] The bulk storage of liquid petroleum gas, petroleum and oil must be in accordance with the recommendations of a Risk Assessment conducted by a Qualified Person. [56722] Exit signs are required at each Emergency Exit location [56059] • Directional exit signage must be provided when the exit is not immediately visible. [56060] • Signage must be illuminated by normal and Emergency Lighting that automatically comes on when the power supply to the normal lighting provision fails. [56061] Emergency power must be provided to illuminate signage for a minimum of 60 minutes. [56062] A diagram showing the emergency exit path to the nearest emergency exit must be displayed on the room side of the guest room door. [56052] Must be in local language(s) and English [56054] All fire safety signage must be in the local language(s) and English. [56308] A means of warning guests with impaired hearing in the event of a General Alarm or voice evacuation message must be provided. [56366] Why is this important? The potential for fire in sleeping accommodation, including hotels, is a significant risk . Whilst building systems (such as sprinklers, fire alarms, and passive fire safety controls) contribute the mitigation of risk, it is the action of people that is often most vital to controlling or escaping the risk in case of a fire. IHG-branded hotels must have well defined and well implemented management arrangements to contribute to the prevention of fire, and to enable prompt and effective response in case of a fire. Operational Requirements Safety & Security S&S/ FireSafety /OR/FSM/ Doc1.1/Nov24 2/12 All hotels are required to adhere to IHGs Brand Safety Standards (BSS) and IHG Managed hotels are also required to adhere to the above Operational Requirements (ORs) - except where local regulations (e.g. OSHA, EU H&S Directives ) exceed either BSS or ORs . Where this is the case, it is the responsibility of the local hotel to develop and implement modified arrangements that satisfy the intent of IHGs BSS/ORs whilst complying with local regulatory requirements or expectations. Supporting Templates and further Guidance and Training can be found in the Fire Safety section of the Responsible Business Portal. IHG M anaged Hotel leadership teams must also adhere to the following Operational Requirements : FSM - 001 Conduct a fire risk assessment , implementing additional controls where required to m anage fire safety risk(s) . Guidance Safety & Security S&S/ FireSafety /OR/FSM/ Doc1.1/Nov24 3/12 Guidance Documented emergency and evacuation plan [BSS - 55945] Every hotel should have a documented and well -practiced emergency response plan in case of known or suspected fire. This plan should consider: • Specific roles of hotel leadership team members or shift supervisors • How the plan will be executed during ‘out of hours’ periods (i.e. 03:00 AM) • All potential people who might be on property in case of emergency, including; o Colleagues o Contractors o Guests, including guests with mobility or sensory impairment Alarm activation Usually the emergency and evacuation response plan will be triggered by activation of the fire alarm. Depending on how your hotel fire alarm is programmed, this might include an alarm signal at the fire alarm panel only, providing colleagues with an ‘investigation period’ (to determine whether the signal is indeed a fire or not), before the full audible hotel -wide alarm begins sounding. Where a general fire alarm is sounded – except as part of a test - evacuation of the property or fire zone (where the alarm is phased/zoned) should commence. The fire alarm should not be silenced or reset until a full inspection has been conducted to determine that no fire exists or following instruction from the Fire Department . Following the incident, the hotel should submit an incident report, using Riskonnect, containing all pertinent information concerning the fire. Considering mobility or sensory impairment Some hotel occupants may find it more challenging to self -evacuate in case of fire. Hotels should consider this population as part of the overall evacuation plan. One tactic to support safe evacuation in case of fire is to agree a ‘Personal Emergency Evacuation Plan’ with the person(s) affected, setting out what action will be taken in case of fire to support evacuation. This is not always practical (for example, if individuals do not volunteer that they have sensory impairment). The hotel might also rely on technology, such as strobe lighting connected to the fire alarm in certain areas or accessible rooms, which flash in case of fire alarm (for any guests or colleagues who have hearing impairments). Unless explicitly agreed with the relevant Fire Department, hotel leadership should assume initial responsibility for support safe evacuation of all building occupants, including those with impairment. Further control tactics that might support safe and prompt evacuation for this population might include: Guidance Safety & Security S&S/ FireSafety /OR/FSM/ Doc1.1/ Nov24 4/12 Procedures for Visually Impaired Guests: • Accommodate on lower floors near exits where possible. • Where reasonable, colleagues should offer to familiarise the guest(s) with emergency exits • Large print notices should accompany Braille notices. • A helper should assist with stair descents and remain with the guest once evacuated until the emergency is over wherever reasonable and safe to do so. Procedures for Hearing- Impaired Guests: • Consider providing alarms with visual or vibrating alerts, such as vibrating pillows. • In case of alarm, colleagues should check on hearing- impaired guests - where reasonable - to ensure their safety. Procedures for Wheelchair Users or Mobility -Impaired Individuals: • Refuge areas should be used, and colleagues should assist in evacuation, waiting for stairs to clear if needed. Refuge areas provide a safer temporary waiting area, that is fire separated from other parts of the building. • Wheelchairs may need to be left behind, and arrangements for moving individuals without their chairs should be made. • Evacuation chairs and other methods may be used; these should form part of the planned emergency evacuation plan and be well practiced by relevant colleagues . Fire risk assessment (FSM – 001) A Fire Risk Assessment (FRA) is a careful examination of the potential causes of fire, the potential for fire to spread and the measures required to extinguish and control the development of a fire. The FRA enables hotel leadership to determine if additional requirements may need to be implemented. An FRA should be hotel -specific, completed by a Competent Person and subject to regular review (typically, reviewed once per year) A competent person is someone with sufficient training and experience or knowledge and skills to be able to advise on the implementation of preventative and protective measures correctly . This person could be an appropriately trained colleague or a third party. The FRA should evaluate the whole hotel , including outdoor locations and any rooms and areas that are rarely used. Some hotels can be assessed in one exercise; however, in much larger hotels it may be helpful to divide them into areas or a series of assessments. Where the hotel has additional facilities that may increase fire risk , special attention should be given to these areas. These areas could include bars, nightclubs and facilities located in the basement or sub- basement with limited means of escape. In performing an FRA, there are inherent limits to the extent of assessment – for example, it might not be possible to confirm the integrity of fire separating material, when hidden behind partition walls or suspended ceilings. These circumstances further highlight the value of a Competent Person, who can use regional judgement and sample- based checks to evaluate the likely adequacy of fire partitions. Guidance Safety & Security S&S/ FireSafety /OR/FSM/ Doc1.1/Nov24 5/12 Non-exhaustive summary of considerations for a FRA FIRE SAFETY RISK ASSESSMENT 1. Identify fire hazards Identify: Sources of ignition Sources of fuel (including stored bulk fuel, such as LPG) Sources of oxygen. Presence of hazardous substances (including oxidizing chemicals) Adjacent businesses or premises that present unusual or heightened fire risk 2. Identify people at risk Identify : People in and around the premises People who are especially at risk (such as those with mobility or sensory impairment) 3. Evaluate, remove, reduce and protect from risk Evaluate the risk of a fire occurring Evaluate the risk to people from fire Remove or reduce fire hazards Remove or reduce the risks to people - Detection and visual and audible alarm notifications - Firefighting - Escape routes - Normal and emergency l ightin g - Signs and notices - Maintenance of systems relevant to fire safety or fire prevention 4. Record , Plan , Inform, instruct and train Record significant findings and actions taken and further action require Share the significant findings with relevant people Use the conclusions of the fire risk assessment to inform any changes to the emergency evacuation plan 5. Review. Keep assessment under review Revise where necessary, such as in case of fire incident or hotel renovations Remember to keep your fire risk assessment under review. Per step 4. above, the FRA is likely to identify some improvement opportunities. This might include physical works; for example installing an additional smoke detector in a storage room that might previously have been missed when the alarm system was first ins talled. Hotel leadership should ensure that actions arising from the FRA are agreed, resources and an expected timeline for implementation agreed, and then tracked to completion. The following sections provide non- exhaustive guidance for consideration as part of the FRA : Guidance Safety & Security S&S/ FireSafety /OR/FSM/ Doc1.1/ Nov24 6/12 Means of Escape Escape routes and stairways should always be kept clear and free of any obstructions. Corridors, stairways and aisles should be free of temporary or permanent blockages such as chairs, tables, linen, trays, trolleys or trash. Non-conventional means of escape should be evaluated as part of the Competent Person’s FRA of the hotel. This evaluation should also consider the risk that despite signage or other controls, hotel occupants may attempt to use these non -conventional means o f escape. For example: • Escalators are not considered an acceptable means of escape. Escalators should be provided with an emergency stop button and should slow down and stop in the event of an evacuation alarm or the activation of the emergency stop button. • Where ramps are provided as part of an escape route, they should have an easy gradient not steeper than 1 in 12, be provided with handrails and have a non -slip surface. • Portable and "throw -out" ladders, automatic lowering devices, ropes, chutes and other manual devices are not normally acceptable as a means of escape. • Elevators and hoists are not acceptable for means of escape. However, suitably protected evacuation elevators may be acceptable for use by vulnerable guests . Escape via wall or floor hatches, vertical or raking ladders and spiral stairways should only be acceptable in exceptional circumstances and where local regulations permit, for example, as an alternative exit from a plant room due to structural difficulties , and should not be used by guests. Roof exits should only be accepted in exceptional circumstances and should not be used by guests. Doors on escape routes should be regularly maintained and tested monthly. A record of the maintenance and testing should be kept available for inspection for at least three years. Storage should not be allowed on emergency egress stairs; fire -resisting doors and smoke detection should be provided in storerooms opening into emergency egress stairs and self - closers should be provided and maintained i n storerooms. Storerooms should always be kept locked. Storage areas that adjoin emergency egress stairs should be avoided, however , if necessary, the storage space should be fire- rated with the installation of fire- resistant doors equipped with self-closing devices. The doors should be fire- rated to a minimum of 60 minutes to prevent the passage of smoke to the stairs. Items which pose a potential fire risk, even if they do not cause an obstruction, should be prohibited in escape routes and stairways. Examples include heaters (portable or fixed), storage of any type, coat racks and electrical equipment. Electromagnetic door devices Electromagnetic door holders used to hold doors open on escape routes should be linked to the fire alarm and detection system, including a manual release at the door and be included in the fire alarm system test program. The door should be released by one of the following: • Activation of a local fire detector • Activation of a manual fire alarm call point • Any fault or loss of power to the fire alarm and detection system Guidance Safety & Security S&S/ FireSafety /OR/FSM/ Doc1.1/ Nov24 7/12 Electromagnetic door locks should only be used on doors where there is a need for greater security and must be configured to allow unimpeded escape in case of emergency or fire. Electromagnetic door locks that form part of an evacuation route should: • Release on activation of the fire alarm or failure of the power supply . • Be provided with a manual override adjacent to the door . • Be provided with a warning notice and operating instructions. Liquified Petroleum Gas LPG (propane and butane) is highly flammable and heavier than air and, therefore, if a leak occurs it may collect in drains, cellars and basements. When mixed with air, LPG will form an explosive atmosphere which may be ignited by a naked flame or spark. There are two forms of LPG storage typically used in hotels: • Cylinders, for use with portable appliances . • Bulk storage in fixed cylinders, a storage tank or sphere supplied to the hotel by fixed pipework . Hotels should restrict LPG portable appliances to: • Flambé cooking trolleys, lamps and carving trolleys . • Engineer ’s soldering lamps . • Contractor ’s equipment for which a ‘ Hot Work Permit ’ should be in place when in use • External patio space heaters. Numbers of LPG cylinder stored should be kept to a minimum and general guidance for the storage of LPG cylinders should be as follows: • Outside and remote from the hotel in a secure cage or store. • In a separate store apart from other flammable materials, chemicals or other gas cylinders. • Away from areas used by guests . • Away from ignition sources . • With a level, compacted or paved floor kept clear of weeds or vegetation (without the use of weed killers containing chemicals such as sodium chlorate) . • At least 3m (10ft) from any drain. • With a warning symbol and a notice with the words "HIGHLY FLAMMABLE GAS. NO SMOKING. NO NAKED LIGHTS" in conspicuous plain letters . • A water, multi -purpose foam or dry powder extinguisher should be provided near to the store. There may be a small discharge of gas when changing cylinders, so change all cylinders: • Outside and remote from the hotel . • Away from areas used by guests . • Away from sources of ignition. Bulk storage of LPG must be in accordance with the recommendations of a Risk Assessment conducted by a Qualified Person. Dry saunas General safety precautions for dry saunas include: • Saunas should be constructed and installed in accordance with the manufacturer ’s Instructions . Guidance Safety & Security S&S/ FireSafety /OR/FSM/ Doc1.1/ Nov24 8/12 • Where a sprinkler system is installed in the hotel, the sauna cabin should be fitted with a high- temperature sprinkler head. • Electrical installations should be protected by Ground Fault Circuit Interrupters (GFCI) / Residual Current Devices (RCD) in the form of circuit breakers or protected outlets . • Controls should not be accessible to bathers and should be locked where necessary . Maintenance should be carried out in accordance with the manufacturer ’s instructions Service periods of 6 or 12 months are usual, depending on usage and should include: • A general check on the structure for signs of excessive wear and tear . • A check of the electrical installation - including thermostats, high- temperature safety thermostats, heating elements, timers, residual current devices and circuit breakers . • A check of and replacement of damaged or broken stones with similar or recommended stones. The hotel should regularly inspect dry saunas and perform start and end of day inspections including checking for fire risk including combustible items or signs of scorching. Recorded end of day procedures should include ensuring that the sauna is turned OFF and cannot be re-activated by a guest or user. Smoking All hotels should have a colleague smoking policy that is enforced with smoking permitted only in designated areas. Colleagues should be informed as part of their initial training of the smoking policy and the location of the designated smoking areas. It is recommended that an appropriate portable fire extinguisher is made available in the immediate vicinity of the designated smoking area to extinguish any small fires. Fire Doors Fire doors should be reviewed as part of the inspection regime; they may be labelled to indicate their performance characteristics in case of fire. Whilst it is not reasonable to inspect every door as part of the FRA, the Competent Person should stay alert to the general condition of doors (are cold smoke seals intact , for example), how the doors are being used (are they wedged open) and any obvious maintenance issues (are the door closers working as expected to cause the doors to latch shut. Emergency Escape Lighting Emergency lighting is required to enable persons of all ages to evacuate the hotel safely. Automatic emergency lighting may be provided by either self -contained battery -powered luminaries, a central battery system or a generator. Emergency lighting is generally classified into two groups, however , regional differences and terminology may exist : • Non-maintained emergency lighting is designed to turn on in the event of a power failure. It is linked to the building’ s lighting circuitry and reacts to a power failure ensuring emergency exit routes remain illuminated. This type of emergency lighting is mostly found in the workplace, where people are familiar with the escape routes. Guidance Safety & Security S&S/ FireSafety /OR/FSM/ Doc1.1/ Nov24 9/12 • Maintained lighting is designed to be lit continuously and should continue to work even in the event of a power failure. This allows the unit to double as a standard light fitting but still supply the necessary backup in the event of a power outage. This t ype of emergency lighting is often found in public places such as conference areas, nightclubs, hotel corridors, and communal guest areas . The FRA should consider where emergency lighting is provided throughout the hotel, and whether that would likely provide sufficient visibility over evacuation routes in case of emergency. Evacuation and exit signage Means of emergency egress should be clearly visible and coherent to occupants of the hotel to identify the direction of escape. Adequate and reliable exit signage should be provided. The effectiveness of sign age may be adversely affected by several factors , such as : • Placing too many signs too close together should be avoided • Two illuminated signs which are likely to be confused should not be used at the same time • An illuminated sign should not be used in the proximity of another similar illuminated source • Poor design, insufficient number, incorrect positioning, poor state of repair or incorrect functioning of the signs. Signs should be cleaned, maintained, checked and repaired, and if necessary, replaced on a regular basis to ensure that they retain their intrinsic and functional qualities. Exits should be clearly labelled, and care should be taken to ensure directional arrows point in the correct direction, towards the exit. Doors that could be mistaken for an exit should be clearly marked "NOT AN EXIT" or should be marked by a sign indicati ng its actual use, for example, "STORAGE ROOM". Exit signs should meet the following requirements: • Rectangular or square shape • Of sufficient size so that they can easily be seen from all areas. Otherwise, additional signs should be provided • A white pictogram on a green or red background, with the green/red background taking up at least 50% of the area of the sign • Provided with a directional arrow indicating the way to the exit, unless the sign is located at the exit • Text may be provided but it should be supplementary to the pictogram sign Apart from within guestrooms, at least one exit sign should be visible from any point in the hotel. Where possible, the route to an alternative exit should also be indicated, however signs should not be provided in positions that may be contradictory or confusing. Signs should be placed at least 2m (6.5ft) above floor level. At a doorway where, due to low ceiling height, it is not possible to locate a sign immediately above the door, the sign should be placed at the highest possible point next to the door. Care should be taken to ensure that decorations, furnishings or equipment do not obscure the sign. Guidance Safety & Security S&S/ FireSafety /OR/FSM/ Doc1.1/ Nov24 10/12 Signs are not required to be internally illuminated and provided signs are adequately lit by normal and emergency lighting this should be satisfactory. This means that simple signs, for example rigid or semi -rigid plastic signs, may be used at significantl y lower cost and can be installed by hotel personnel. Exit signs connected to or provided with a battery -operated emergency illumination source, should be tested and maintained in accordance with the manufacturer’s instructions. Elevator fire safety signage A professionally prepared sign in the local language(s) and in English with a clear warning against the use of lifts/ elevators in the event of fire, should be provided adjacent to the call button(s) in lift/elevator lobbies, this should read: 'In the event of fire do not use lift/elevator; use stairs' Firefighting equipment signage Where fire -fighting equipment cannot be seen from all areas because, for example, the equipment is hidden in recessed fire points or cupboards, a sign should be displayed indicating its location. Fire- fighting equipment signs should: • Be rectangular or square. • Have a white pictogram on a red background, with the red background taking up at least 50% of the area of the sign. • Where the fire -fighting equipment does not have details of its use and method of operation, a sign giving clear and concise details should be provided. Evacuation route signage Evacuation plans should be clearly posted in all guestrooms. These notices should include but are not necessarily limited to: • Symbols indicating fire alarm pull station locations • Symbols indicating fire extinguisher locations • Symbols indicating fire hose locations • An arrow or dot indicating to the guest "YOU ARE HERE." • All fire exits clearly indicated. • The floor plan should be facing the way a guest would read a plan in their room, so that the fire exits are in the proper direction (left or right) when a guest leaves the room. Example Fire Emergency Evacuation Plan: Guidance Safety & Security S&S/ FireSafety /OR/FSM/ Doc1.1/ Nov24 11/12 Tented Structures (marquees etc.) A specific FRA should be conducted when tented structures are used. The risk assessment can help the hotel identify potential hazards and create the appropriate control measures. The fire safety measures in a tented structure should be as good as the fire safety measures within the hotel. This may include scheduling additional colleagues for the tented structure. It should be noted that approval by the hotel ’s local Authority Having Jurisdiction (AHJ) may be required before erecting a tented structure. General points for consideration when erecting a tented structure: • The site layout • Access for emergency vehicles • Fabrics used for the construction of the tented structure • Means of egress • Firefighting equipment • Fire alarms • Lighting • General fire safety There should be a plan showing the position of all entrances, exits, generators and vehicles and the location of the tented structure in relation to the hotel. In addition: • There should be a clear space of at least 6m (20ft) between each tented structure • Grass and other vegetation should be kept as short as possible. • Generators, garbage, parked vehicles, petroleum gas, cylinder storage and other fire hazards should be at least 6m (20ft) away from the tented structures . • Firefighting vehicles should be able to access within 50m (165ft) of the tented structure. The fabric of tented structures, including any linings, should be durabl e, flame retardant and should not support combustion, form burning droplets or produce significant quantities of smoke and gases. There should be no dead -end conditions. One suitable fire extinguisher should be provided for small structures (those holding no more than 15 people). Larger structures should have a minimum of two extinguishers, one for every 200m ² (2153 ft ²) or part thereof. The extinguishers should be placed to help ensure maximum travel is less than 30m (100ft) to reach the extinguisher and should be in prominent positions near exits where they can be easily seen. Tented structures should be equipped with a device which warns persons in the event of a fire. The hotel should also consider the best method to notify emergency services (for example, a portable radio or phone). Hotel colleagues should be aware of the nearest available telephone. If the tented structure is used outside of daylight hours, emergency lighting should be installed. Special effects using flame, heat and pyrotechnics should be prohibited in and around tented structures. Open flame apparatus such as heaters , cookers , fire pits, and heat lamps should be prohibited in tented structures. Guidance Safety & Security S&S/ FireSafety /OR/FSM/ Doc1.1/Nov24 12/12 Training [BSS - 55945, continued] General fire safety training should be provided to all colleagues, this training should include: • A summary of any significant findings from your hotel -specific FRA, and what control measures have been put in place to manage the risk(s). • Information on how to control fire hazards within the hotel. This may include handling and storage of flammable materials, use of electrical equipment, housekeeping practices, and the regular testing and maintenance of fire safety systems. • Ensure that all colleagues are aware of emergency procedures when responding to a fire in the hotel. This should include an understanding of the fire alarm system, communication during an emergency, and liaising with appropriate individuals. Evacuation procedures should be tested regularly, all colleagues should participate on a six - monthly basis ; these tests (or ‘drills’) also form part of colleague training. Specific training requirements on emergency and evacuation procedure(s) may depend on several factors , including how many defined roles are required to successfully complete an evacuation according to the hotel specific emergency and evacuation plan (i.e., what is the minimum number of people required to complete the plan as written). In deciding how many colleagues to train in these particular duties, sufficient numbers should be trained to cover for leave and colleague sick absence. All training should be recorded by the hotel, including a copy of the training materials used, the name and date of the trainer, and the name, role and date of those attending the training. Ten Minute Trainers Safety & Security S&S/Health&Safety/TMT/ ICP/Doc3. 2/Sep24 1 Ten Minute Trainer Legionella This programme is designed to introduce employees to legionella, what it is and where it is found. The methods of prevention and understand why record keeping is important. Target audience All staff. Training Tip: Read through the materials; if you plan to issue the Participant Handout and Quiz, print out sufficient copies. Welcome everyone to the session, introduce anyone who is new and encourage everyone to ask questions and join in the discussion. Explain that the purpose of these sessions is to make them feel conf ident in their work and make sure they know what to do to carry out their work safely and responsibly. Explain that at the end of the session there will be a quiz and a record of attendance and understanding to be signed to help us record who has been trained. _________________________________________________________________________ What is Legionella? The bacterium Legionella pneumophila and related bacteria are common in natural water sources such as rivers, lakes and reservoirs, but usually in low numbers. They may also be found in purpose -build water systems such as cooling towers, evaporative condensers, hot and cold -water systems and spa pools. This bacterium can be inhaled deep into the lungs as an aerosol and can cause Legionnaires Disease , a pneumonia -like infection. What helps Legionella to grow? Water conditions that tend to promote the growth of Legionella include: • Stagnation • Temperatures between 20° and 50°C. The optimal growth range is 35° -46°C • pH level between 5.0 and 8.5 • Sediment th at tends to promote growth of commensal microflora • Micro -organisms including algae, flavobacteria, and Pseudomonas, which supply essential nutrients for growth of Legionella or harbor the organism . Where can Legionella be found? There are many potential so urces of Legionnaire’s disease in the hotel environment. Some of these sources are: • Evaporative cooling towers Ten Minute Trainers Safety & Security S&S/Health&Safety/TMT/ ICP/Doc3. 2/Sep24 2 • Hot and cold -water systems • Spa pools and whirlpool baths/ hot tubs; • Water softeners and deioni sers • Showers (guest rooms / pools etc) • Lawn sprinklers and hoses • Fountains and water features • Irrigation systems, • Fire, dust and odour suppression systems. All have capacity to generate water droplets (aerosols) during operation and some, may dispense them directly into an individual’s breathing zon e. Each possible source should have a control and testing regime to lessen the possibility of transmitting and/or cultivating Legionnaire’s disease. Methods of Prevention The list below provides some methods of prevention of Legionella (not exhaustive) • Ensure that the hot water temperature for calorifiers and hot water storage vessels are maintained at a temperature at or above60oC and this temperature does not fall below 50oC at any point within the circulation pipe work • Avoid stagnation • Maintain stringent cleanliness of water systems and ventilation systems • Use of the proper water treatment regime in wet cooling towers • Introduce the correct level of maintenance to ensure correct and safe operation and compliance with statutory regulations • Reduce the amount of water stored (24 hours maximum) • Keep all water storage systems clean and sealed from extraneous matter and maintain temperatures below 20°C for cold -water services. A suitable and sufficient legionella risk assessment should be carried o ut by a competent person. If the necessary competence, knowledge and expertise does not exist internally, there may be a need to appoint someone externally to carry out the legionella risk assessment. The risk assessment will need to reviewed regularly and specifically when there is reason to believe that the original risk assessment may no longer be valid. The review should also include management and communication procedures as appropriate. Record keeping All maintenance, modifications, inspections, and s afety/health training related to building water systems (i.e. internal and third party) should be documented and maintained. Written records must be maintained and kept for at least 3 years or more Information and feedback on training materials contact: BRRLearningandDevelopment@ihg.com Ten Minute Trainers Safety & Security S&S/Health&Safety/TMT/ ICP/Doc3. 2/Sep24 3 Quiz 1. Where can Legionella bacteria be found in the hotel environment? a) Evaporative cooling towers b) Spa pools and whirlpool baths/hot tubs c) Hot & cold water systems d) Showers (guest rooms/pods) e) All of the above 5. How long should written records be kept and maintained for? a) 2 years b) 3 years c) 5 years 2. What helps Legionella grow? a) Stagnation b) Sediment that tends to promote the growth of commensal microflora c) Temperature between 20C and 50C d) All of the above 3. Legionella pneumophila and related bacteria can be inhaled deep into the lungs as an aerosol? a) True b) False 4. Who should carry out the legionella risk assessment? a) Somone from the hotel b) A third-party contractor c) Either of the above depending on who is most competent. When you have completed this quiz, turn it in to your supervisor. Name: ______________________________________ Date: ______________________________________ Ten Minute Trainers Safety & Security S&S/Health&Safety/TMT/ ICP/Doc3. 2/Sep24 4 Quiz Answers 1. (e) All of the above. 2. (d) All of the above 3. (a) True 4. (c) Either depending on who is most competent 5.
